title: B2B AI Knowledge & Workflow Platform
summary: An internal enterprise AI platform for managing organizations, roles, bots, and documents with RAG-powered chat and MCP tool integration. I built the Next.js frontend and MCP server from scratch as the sole developer for both.

projectIntro.title: Project overview
projectIntro.description: Administrators configure organizations, roles, bots, and documents; users select a bot for their task and converse with it. Responses are generated through document-grounded retrieval and model calls, while agents can invoke MCP tools when needed. I designed the frontend and MCP-connected UI so those steps read as one product flow.

workflow.title: Primary user flow
workflow.description: After an administrator configures bots and document context, users select a bot, ask a question, and follow streaming responses and tool output in one conversation.

architecture.title: I separated administration, AI chat, and MCP tools into role-specific services.
architecture.description: The frontend delivers server data through App Router rendering and React Query hydration, while feature-local Zustand stores hold UI-only state. The API owns authentication, organizations, roles, bots, and chat history; the AI service owns RAG and LLM response generation; the MCP server exposes tools, resources, and prompts to AI agents.
architecture.alt: Platform architecture connecting the Next.js frontend, internal API, AI RAG service, MCP server, Qdrant, and LLM providers
architecture.caption: The overall structure separates the user product path from the AI agent's MCP tool-call path.

implementation.title: I made AI features understandable and operable as one product flow.
implementation.description: Administration, bot-specific chat, UI state, and MCP execution each have distinct responsibilities. These four cases explain how I designed and implemented those frontend boundaries.

admin.title: I organized organization, role, and bot administration by feature.
admin.context: Administrators need to manage organization-specific permissions, AI bots, prompts, and documents while understanding the scope of each change.
admin.problem: When operational targets and permission conditions are spread across many screens, it becomes difficult to understand which feature controls which data and access.
admin.decision: I separated organizations, permissions, bots, prompts, and documents into feature-based administration surfaces. Authentication and authorization stay in the server-data path, while each view centers on its operational target.
admin.result: Administrators can manage each setting in role-appropriate views, and frontend capabilities can grow by domain.
admin.flow: Authentication → organization and permission check → administration feature → manage bots, prompts, and documents

chat.title: I rendered bot-specific AI generation as a continuous conversation.
chat.context: Users select a bot for a work task and need to follow both generated output and the final response in the same conversation context.
chat.problem: Mixing settings and chat state for multiple bots globally can leave the wrong bot configuration behind or make streaming timing inconsistent across screens.
chat.decision: I scoped chat settings to dynamic bot routes and appended API SSE responses to the generated answer on screen. Chat history and bot-specific settings stay behind separate boundaries.
chat.result: Users follow generated and finalized responses in the context of the bot they selected, while each bot chat stays independent.
chat.flow: Select bot → bot-scoped route and settings → receive SSE → render generating answer → conversation history

content.title: I separated server data from UI state.
content.context: Administration and chat screens use organization, bot, and document data from the server alongside filters, selections, and panel state in the current view.
content.problem: Putting server data and temporary UI state in one store makes cache updates and screen interaction affect each other, making state harder to trace as features grow.
content.decision: Server Actions and React Query prefetching and hydration deliver server state. Feature-local Zustand stores hold view-only state such as filters, selections, and panels.
content.result: Data refresh and screen-interaction responsibilities are separate and traceable by feature. Server rendering and client interaction work inside their respective boundaries.
content.flow: Server Actions → React Query prefetch and hydration → server data → feature-local UI store → view interaction

mcp.title: I built the MCP server and progress-aware tool experience from scratch.
mcp.context: When AI agents call business tools, users need to understand not only the result but also the progress of longer-running work.
mcp.problem: Short general tool calls and long pipelines such as meeting minutes require different connection lifecycles and progress delivery.
mcp.decision: I built the server with Express and the MCP SDK: stateless transport for general tools, and session-specific transport with SSE progress for the meeting-minutes pipeline. Tools, resources, and prompts use an extensible registration structure.
mcp.result: AI agents can call business capabilities through standard MCP paths, while users can follow progress and final output for long-running work inside the product flow.
mcp.flow: AI agent → choose MCP transport → tools, resources, and prompts → SSE progress or immediate result → product UI

result.title: I connected AI and administration capabilities into one product flow.
result.description: Administration, RAG-powered bot chat, and MCP execution each operate behind explicit responsibility boundaries. I also completed web-standard, accessibility, and performance improvements and added axe-based Playwright checks for core screens at desktop and mobile viewports.
